title: Biomechanical Measurement & Technology
theme: Marker and markerless capture, force plates, IMUs, EMG, video and tracking — and the statistics of measurement error
question: When does a biomechanical number tell you something true, precise and useful enough about one athlete to act on?

overview.text: Every claim in the rest of this course rests on a measurement. Before you can evaluate whether trunk rotation timing relates to velocity, or whether a drill changed a swing, you need to know how the number was produced, how far it might be from the truth, and how much it would vary if nothing had changed. This week treats measurement as a scientific problem in its own right, with its own physics, its own error structure and its own literature.

The first four lessons take the instruments in turn. Marker-based capture locates skin markers precisely but models bones, joint centres and angles; markerless capture moves biomechanics into the game by inferring joints from video, at the cost of system-specific offsets; force plates, inertial sensors and EMG each measure one thing directly and infer the rest; video and stadium tracking are limited by frame rate and geometry and describe the ball and bat rather than the body. For each, you will identify where systematic and random error enter and what the instrument cannot measure at all.

The fifth lesson supplies the statistics — typical error, ICC forms, Bland–Altman limits of agreement and minimal detectable change — and the laboratory lets you manipulate bias, random error, within-athlete variability and true change to see when an apparent mechanical change is real. The case is a critique of a published markerless validation study, and the assignment is a procurement memo that decides whether a fictional field system is fit for a specific development decision. Throughout, the standard is the same: a measured difference is not a deficiency, a mechanical change is not an improvement, and a joint moment is not an injury probability.

objectives: Explain how each technology produces its outputs and where systematic and random error enter.
Interpret validation and agreement studies, including bias and limits of agreement.
Calculate typical error, ICC-based reliability and minimal detectable change.
Judge whether an observed change exceeds measurement error and within-athlete variability.
Evaluate a vendor claim or biomechanics report before acting on it.

lessons.title: Marker-Based Motion Capture
lessons.summary: How optical marker systems turn reflections into joint angles, and where systematic and random error enter at each step from calibration to filtering.
objectives: Trace the processing chain from camera calibration to joint angles and identify the error that enters at each stage.
Compare predictive and functional joint-centre methods and explain why soft-tissue artifact limits both.
Select and defend a filter cut-off using residual analysis, and quantify how differentiation amplifies noise.
lessons.executive: Marker-based capture is the laboratory reference for pitching and hitting kinematics, but it is not a direct measurement of bone. Cameras locate reflective markers on skin to within about a millimetre; everything after that — segment frames, joint centres, rotation sequences, filtering — is modelling. The largest error is usually soft tissue moving relative to bone, not camera noise. Two laboratories can report different shoulder external-rotation values for the same pitch because they use different marker sets, joint-centre methods and angle definitions. Before comparing numbers across reports, ask which model, which sequence and which filter produced them.

explore.text: Two laboratories test the same synthetic right-handed pitcher a week apart. Laboratory A reports peak shoulder external rotation of 178°; Laboratory B reports 164°. Both use twelve-camera optical systems sampling at 240 Hz, both report sub-millimetre calibration residuals, and the pitcher's fastball velocity is unchanged. A coach reads the two reports and concludes that the pitcher has lost 14° of layback. The data are synthetic; the situation is common.
Before reading on, list every step between a reflective marker on the skin and the number 178°. At which steps could two well-run laboratories legitimately disagree?

The answer is that nearly every step after marker reconstruction involves a modelling choice. The cameras see markers, not bones. A segment's orientation is inferred from a cluster of markers; a joint centre is inferred from landmarks or from movement; a joint angle is a particular decomposition of the relative orientation of two segment frames; and the peak is read from a filtered, differentiated signal. Each choice is defensible, and each changes the number. A 14° gap between laboratories therefore says nothing, by itself, about the pitcher. This lesson builds the chain step by step so that you can ask the questions that reveal whether two numbers are comparable.

understand.text: From reflections to 3D marker trajectories

An optical system uses infrared cameras that emit light and detect it reflected from retro-reflective markers. Each camera reports the 2D image coordinates of every marker it sees. Calibration — typically a static frame that defines the global axes and a wand of known length moved through the capture volume — estimates each camera's position, orientation and lens parameters. Once at least two calibrated cameras see the same marker, its 3D position is reconstructed by triangulation, and the residual (how far the camera rays miss one another) is an index of reconstruction quality. Trajectories are then labelled, and short gaps where too few cameras saw a marker are interpolated.

Notice what calibration residuals do and do not tell you. A residual of 0.5 mm says the rays intersect well; it says nothing about whether the marker was placed on the intended landmark, whether the skin moved, or whether a gap was filled with a plausible but invented curve. Reconstruction accuracy is the best-controlled error in the chain and usually the smallest.
From markers to segments, joint centres and angles

Each body segment is treated as a rigid body. Three or more non-collinear markers define a technical frame for the segment; anatomical landmarks, palpated or digitized in a static trial, define an anatomical frame tied to bony features. Joint centres are needed to define segment axes and, later, to compute joint moments. The International Society of Biomechanics publishes recommended coordinate systems and rotation sequences for each joint — for the shoulder, elbow, wrist and hand in Wu et al. — so that angles from different laboratories mean the same thing.

Joint-centre estimation follows two families of methods. **Predictive** (regression) methods place the centre from anatomical landmarks using equations derived from cadaver or imaging samples — for instance, locating the hip centre as proportions of pelvic width and depth. **Functional** methods estimate the centre from the movement itself: when one segment rotates relative to its neighbour about a ball joint, the markers on the moving segment lie on spheres about a common point, and least-squares fitting recovers that point. Ehrig and colleagues compared formal functional methods and proposed a symmetrical approach (SCoRE) that does not require one segment to be stationary; in their test conditions most methods located the centre to within about 0.3 cm when the range of motion was at least 45°.

The practical trade-off follows. Predictive methods need only a static trial and are robust when the athlete cannot or will not perform a calibration movement, but they inherit the population and the imaging method of the equations. Functional methods individualize the estimate, but they need a sufficient range of motion, they are sensitive to soft-tissue artifact during the calibration movement, and their accuracy in a simulation is an upper bound on accuracy in a pitcher. The glenohumeral centre, which cannot be palpated and moves with the scapula, is the joint where this choice matters most for pitching.

understand.title: Prerequisite: a joint angle is a rotation decomposition

blocks.text: A joint angle in 3D is not measured; it is computed. The relative orientation of the distal segment's frame with respect to the proximal frame is a rotation matrix. Expressing that matrix as three angles requires choosing an order of rotations about specified axes — a Cardan or Euler sequence. Different sequences give different numbers for the same orientation, and some sequences become unstable (gimbal lock) near particular postures. Wu et al. recommend a Y–X–Y sequence for humerus relative to thorax; many pitching studies have used other conventions. Week 1 developed this in detail; see [Three-Dimensional Human Movement](#b01-l2).

understand.text: Soft-tissue artifact: the dominant error

Skin markers move relative to the underlying bone because skin slides, muscles contract and change shape, and inertial effects shake soft tissue during fast movement. Leardini and colleagues' review identified this soft-tissue artifact as the most critical source of error in human movement analysis, found that it is subject- and task-specific, and concluded that reliable 3D skeletal kinematics from skin markers had not been fully achieved; compensation by rigid clusters, optimization and joint constraints reduces but does not remove it.

A hypothetical magnitude check. Suppose a marker cluster on the upper arm sits about 40 mm from the humerus's long axis and the skin under it slides 10 mm circumferentially during arm cocking. The apparent rotation about the long axis is roughly the arc divided by the radius: 10/40 = 0.25 rad ≈ 14°. Nothing about the bone moved by that amount. This is why long-axis rotations of segments with thick soft-tissue cover — humeral internal and external rotation, thigh rotation — deserve the least trust, and why reported shoulder external-rotation peaks differ across marker sets.

understand.title: Methodological note: filtering, residual analysis and noise amplification

blocks.text: Marker trajectories contain random noise that is broad-band, while the movement signal is concentrated at low frequencies. Laboratories therefore apply a low-pass filter, commonly a Butterworth filter run forwards and backwards so that no phase lag is introduced. Winter's residual analysis chooses the cut-off by filtering at many frequencies, plotting the root-mean-square difference between raw and filtered data against cut-off frequency, and choosing the frequency where the residual begins to exceed the extrapolated noise line — the point at which signal distortion and remaining noise are balanced.

Why this matters: differentiation amplifies noise. Two markers 100 mm apart define a segment angle; give each an independent 1 mm random error perpendicular to the segment. The angle error is about √2 × 1/100 rad ≈ 0.81°. At 240 Hz, a finite-difference velocity built from two such independent errors carries noise of about 0.81 × √2 × 240 ≈ 275°/s, and the second difference for acceleration carries roughly 0.81 × √6 × 240² ≈ 114,000°/s². A clean-looking angle can produce a meaningless angular acceleration and therefore a meaningless net joint moment.

Filtering creates the opposite problem. Pitching and hitting contain brief, high-frequency events — foot contact, ball release, bat–ball contact. A cut-off low enough to suppress noise also flattens and shifts sharp peaks, so filtered peak velocities can be underestimates. Filtering kinematic and force data at different cut-offs before inverse dynamics can produce spurious moment peaks near impacts, because the two signals no longer describe the same event at the same bandwidth. Ask any report for the cut-off, the filter type, whether it was chosen per signal or fixed, and how impacts were handled.

challenge.text: Calling marker-based capture the gold standard is a convenience, not a fact. Its own validity is established against simpler references — calibration objects of known geometry — and, for bone motion, against invasive or radiographic methods that show substantial soft-tissue artifact. Leardini et al. describe that artifact as the most critical error; Wade et al. note that without a bone-referenced comparison such as biplanar videoradiography the true accuracy of either marker or markerless systems remains unknown. When a markerless system disagrees with a marker system, the disagreement is a difference between two imperfect estimates, and some of it may belong to the marker system.

Reproducibility across laboratories is a second problem. Marker placement depends on the person palpating landmarks; different marker sets, joint-centre methods and rotation sequences yield different values; and reports rarely include enough detail to reconstruct the processing. Much of the pitching canon comes from a small number of laboratories using their own conventions. That consistency is useful within a laboratory and misleading across laboratories.

A third limit is ecological. Laboratory capture requires markers, tight clothing, a controlled volume and often an indoor mound. Pitchers may throw at slightly lower intensity, hitters often hit off a tee or from a machine, and the task loses the perceptual demands of competition. A precise measurement of a modified task may answer a different question from the one the coach is asking.

Triangulation locates skin markers precisely; rigid-body models translate markers into bone orientation.
Reconstruction accuracy is well documented; bone-pin and imaging work summarized by Leardini et al. shows soft-tissue artifact large enough to matter.
True bone kinematics of the throwing shoulder at game speed; the size of soft-tissue artifact in long-axis rotations for a given athlete.
Has changing the variable improved performance?
Not applicable: a measurement system does not improve performance. The question is whether its numbers support a decision that might.
Does the improvement transfer to competition?
Laboratory values may not transfer to the in-game task; the system cannot be used in games.
What are the implications for loading or potential injury-related risk?
Joint moments computed from these kinematics inherit their joint-centre and filtering errors; a moment is not an injury probability.

items: **(1) Biomechanical measurement:** Strongest tier for marker-based capture: reconstruction is precise; segment and joint-angle accuracy is limited by soft tissue and model choices.
**(2) Mechanics → mechanical output:** Many associations between kinematics and ball velocity come from this method; they are cross-sectional and laboratory-bound.
**(3) Mechanics → competitive outcome:** Very few links from laboratory kinematics to competitive outcomes; this is not what the method measures.
**(4) Demonstrated intervention effect:** Measurement does not test interventions; it is the instrument used in intervention studies.
**(5) Retention and transfer:** Retention and transfer require repeated measurement over time, ideally in the competitive setting the laboratory cannot reproduce.

apply.text: Return to the two laboratories. Before accepting a 14° loss of layback, request four things: the marker set and whether the glenohumeral centre was estimated predictively or functionally; the rotation sequence used for the humerus relative to the thorax; the filter type and cut-off; and each laboratory's test–retest typical error for that variable. If the laboratories used different sequences, the values are not on the same scale. If the same laboratory had tested the pitcher twice, a 14° change would be informative only if it exceeded that laboratory's minimal detectable change, which you will calculate in [Reliability, Validity & Measurement Error](#b02-l5).

For hitting, the same logic applies with different weak points. Hand and bat markers are occluded by the body during the swing; the bat is rigid, so its motion is well measured if its markers are visible, but the hands and wrists are small segments where marker spacing is short and angle noise is large. Peak pelvis and trunk angular velocities are robust; wrist and forearm long-axis rotations are fragile.

apply.title: Executive twist: one budget, two laboratories

blocks.text: A development department can fund one marker-based laboratory session per pitcher per year, or buy time at an external laboratory that uses a different model. If the purpose is to follow each athlete's change over time, consistency of method within athletes matters more than the absolute accuracy of any single laboratory. Commit to one model, one processing pipeline and one set of definitions, and document them so that a new analyst produces the same numbers. Comparing an athlete to a published norm from another laboratory is the weakest use of the data.

retain.text: Marker-based capture measures marker positions precisely and infers everything else. The main error is soft tissue, not cameras; joint-centre methods, rotation sequences and filter choices change the numbers; and differentiation multiplies noise while filtering attenuates peaks. Compare numbers only when the pipeline is known and shared.
Name three processing choices that could make two laboratories report different peak shoulder external rotation for the same pitch.
Why does a 1 mm marker error matter more for angular acceleration than for angle?
When would you prefer a functional joint-centre method, and what does it require of the athlete?

takeaways: Cameras locate skin markers precisely; bones, joint centres and angles are modelled.
Soft-tissue artifact is the dominant error and is worst for long-axis rotations of well-covered segments.
Joint-angle values depend on marker set, joint-centre method and rotation sequence, so cross-laboratory comparisons need a shared pipeline.
Differentiation amplifies noise; filtering suppresses it but can attenuate peaks around impacts.

check.explanation: Leardini and colleagues identify soft-tissue artifact — skin and muscle moving relative to bone — as the most critical error. It is task- and subject-specific and cannot be fully compensated, whereas calibration residuals are typically below a millimetre.

optionFeedback.c: Labelling errors are real but usually detectable and correctable during processing.
optionFeedback.d: Sampling rate affects temporal resolution of fast events but is not the dominant error in bone-motion estimates.

check.explanation: The angle error is approximately √2 × (1 mm / 50 mm) rad = 0.0283 rad ≈ 1.6°. Halving marker spacing doubles the angular error, which is why small segments such as the hand and forearm produce noisier angles.

optionFeedback.a: This underestimates; it would require 200 mm spacing.
optionFeedback.b: This is the value for 100 mm spacing, not 50 mm.

check.explanation: Residual analysis plots the RMS difference between raw and filtered signals against cut-off frequency. At high cut-offs the residual reflects noise only; the cut-off is chosen where the residual departs from the extrapolated noise line, so that the distortion of the signal roughly equals the noise left in.

optionFeedback.a: The residual reaches zero only with no filtering at all, which leaves all the noise in.
optionFeedback.c: Content above the Nyquist frequency cannot be represented at all; that is a sampling issue, not a cut-off criterion.
optionFeedback.d: Choosing the cut-off that maximizes peaks selects for noise.

lessons.title: Markerless Motion Capture
lessons.summary: How video-based pose estimation produces 3D kinematics, what agreement studies against marker systems show for pitching, and what the much thinner hitting and in-game evidence can and cannot support.
objectives: Explain how 2D keypoint detection, multi-camera reconstruction and skeletal-model fitting produce markerless joint angles.
Interpret published agreement studies (CMC, mean differences, per-joint position error) and the systematic biases they reveal.
Characterize precisely what the current markerless evidence establishes for in-game pitching and hitting, and what it does not.
lessons.executive: Markerless systems estimate joints from video using neural networks trained on human-labelled images, then fit a skeleton across cameras. They make in-game biomechanics possible, which marker systems cannot. Peer-reviewed comparisons in pitching show similar movement patterns but systematic differences in several joint angles, large enough that each system needs its own norms. Comparisons with bone-referenced methods do not yet exist for baseball. For hitting, there is now large-sample in-game observational research, but we found no peer-reviewed validation of markerless swing kinematics against a laboratory reference. Use markerless data within one system; do not mix systems or treat vendor accuracy statements as validation.

explore.text: A synthetic pitcher's laboratory report (marker-based) shows peak shoulder external rotation of 176°. The in-game report from the stadium's markerless system for his next start shows 165° on fastballs of the same velocity. His pitching coach wants to know whether he has “lose his layback” between the laboratory and the game. Data are synthetic.
List three explanations for an 11° difference that have nothing to do with a change in the pitcher. Then decide what evidence would distinguish them.

There are at least four candidate explanations: a system-specific bias (the two systems define or locate the shoulder differently); the setting (game versus laboratory intensity, clothing, warm-up and arousal); random error in either system; and a genuine change in the athlete. The published literature can estimate the first, partly inform the second, and tell you how big the third is likely to be. Only after subtracting those can you consider the fourth. This lesson is about building that subtraction honestly.

understand.text: How markerless capture produces an angle

Markerless systems replace physical markers with keypoints detected in each camera image by a convolutional neural network. The network is trained on large sets of images in which people have labelled joint locations; it outputs, for each image, the most likely 2D position of each keypoint. With several synchronized, calibrated cameras the 2D detections are triangulated or used to fit a 3D skeletal model, often with constraints on segment lengths and joint degrees of freedom; joint angles are then computed from the fitted segment orientations. Wade and colleagues' scoping review notes a central limitation: open-source pose-estimation models were not designed for biomechanics, and the training labels are visual estimates of joint locations, inconsistently placed, rather than anatomical joint centres.

understand.caption: Markerless pipeline and the assumptions embedded at each step

steps.label: Video
steps.text: Synchronized calibrated cameras; frame rate and exposure set motion blur and temporal resolution.

steps.label: 2D keypoints
steps.text: Network trained on human labels. Assumption: the labelled point corresponds to the joint you care about.

steps.label: 3D reconstruction
steps.text: Triangulation or model fitting across views. Assumption: enough cameras see each joint without occlusion.

steps.label: Skeletal model
steps.text: Segment lengths, joint constraints. Assumption: the model's anatomy fits this athlete.

steps.label: Angles and events
steps.text: Rotation sequence, event detection. Assumption: definitions match the system you compare against.

understand.text: Two consequences follow. First, markerless systems have no soft-tissue artifact in the marker sense, but they have an analogous problem: the network infers joint positions from the visible body surface and clothing, and long-axis rotations — humeral rotation, forearm pronation — are poorly constrained by an outline. Second, every vendor's model is trained and constrained differently, so two markerless systems are not interchangeable with one another any more than with a marker system.
What agreement studies in pitching show

Fleisig and colleagues recorded 275 fastballs from 30 pitchers (mean age about 17 years) simultaneously with a 9-camera markerless system and a 12-camera marker system, both at 240 Hz. Time-series agreement for the waveforms analyzed was high (coefficients of multiple correlation 0.88–0.97), meaning the shapes of the movement patterns were similar, but several discrete values differed systematically between systems. The authors recommended establishing normative ranges separately for each system.

Aguinaldo and colleagues recorded 18 collegiate pitchers simultaneously with a marker-based reference, an in-stadium system (Hawk-Eye) and a portable system (Theia3D). Mean per-joint position errors were 56.6 ± 9.4 mm and 52.0 ± 12.3 mm respectively; stride length agreed best, shoulder rotational variables agreed least, and the authors concluded that camera configuration, deployment and pose-estimation model all affect biomechanical accuracy. They also estimated joint kinetics, which inherit these position errors.

Outside baseball, Kanko and colleagues compared Theia3D with marker-based capture during treadmill walking in 30 adults: joint centres differed by about 2.5 cm or less for most joints (3.6 cm at the hip), angle patterns were similar, and rotations about segment long axes showed the largest differences. One author was the developer company's president, a conflict the preprint disclosed. Walking is slow; agreement in gait is an upper bound, not an estimate, for throwing.

understand.title: Prerequisite: what a coefficient of multiple correlation tells you

blocks.text: The coefficient of multiple correlation (CMC) measures how similar two or more waveforms are in shape across the movement cycle. A CMC near 1 means the curves rise and fall together. It is largely insensitive to a constant offset: a markerless shoulder curve that sits 10° below the marker curve throughout can still have a CMC above 0.9. That is why the same study can report excellent waveform agreement and clinically important differences in peak values. For decisions about individual athletes, you need the bias and limits of agreement for the specific discrete variable, developed in [Reliability, Validity & Measurement Error](#b02-l5).

understand.text: Where systematic bias comes from

A markerless system's offset from a marker system is not one error but several stacked together. The training labels place, say, the shoulder keypoint where annotators judged the shoulder to be in photographs — usually near the visible top of the arm — whereas a marker model places the glenohumeral centre by regression or functional fitting inside the body. The skeletal model then imposes its own segment definitions and joint constraints; if it allows only limited scapular motion, humeral elevation and rotation absorb what the scapula did. Clothing, sleeves and body shape change the visible outline from which keypoints are inferred. Camera number and placement determine how often the throwing arm is occluded by the trunk at maximum external rotation. Event definitions — how foot contact or ball release is detected — shift every time-normalized value. Each of these is systematic for a given installation and software version, which is why a constant offset can coexist with good waveform agreement and why bias can change when the vendor updates its model.

The implication is supported directly by the comparison studies: Aguinaldo and colleagues attributed differences in accuracy to camera configuration, deployment and pose-estimation model, and Wade and colleagues argued that improving training-data labelling and testing against a bone-referenced standard are the necessary next steps for the field.

understand.title: Methodological note: why per-joint position error does not translate directly into angle error

blocks.text: A mean per-joint position error of about 5 cm sounds large, but angle error depends on how errors at the two ends of a segment co-vary. If a model consistently places both the shoulder and elbow 5 cm forward, the upper-arm angle is unchanged; if the errors are independent and perpendicular to a 30 cm segment, the angle error can approach atan(√2 × 5/30) ≈ 13°. Systematic, correlated errors tend to cancel in angles and appear as offsets; independent errors appear as noise. Long-axis rotation is worse still, because it depends on keypoints close to the axis. Per-joint position error is therefore a screening metric; the decision-relevant quantity is the error in the specific angle, at the specific instant, in the specific task.

challenge.text: Laboratory versus in-game measurement

Markerless capture's main advantage is that it works where markers cannot: in games. Giordano and colleagues published in-game reference values from eight synchronized 300-Hz KinaTrax cameras at two NCAA Division I stadiums, for 51 pitchers from five teams during the 2023 season. Jump and colleagues used in-game markerless data from 335 Division I pitchers and statistical parametric mapping to relate hip–shoulder separation to pitch velocity; the association was positive but weak (peak r ≈ 0.16) with substantial differences between individual pitchers.

Whether in-game markerless data can stand in for laboratory capture is unresolved. Lerch and colleagues found that within-pitcher variability across ten fastballs was similar for eight of ten kinematic variables between in-game markerless and laboratory marker-based data, but greater in-game for maximum shoulder external rotation and elbow flexion at that instant, and that mean values differed substantially. Their design compared different pitchers in each condition, so system, setting and sample differences are confounded. Fleisig et al. and Aguinaldo et al. show system-specific offsets even when the same pitch is captured simultaneously.
Hitting: what the evidence currently contains

Markerless hitting research is newer and thinner than pitching research. Hoechstetter and colleagues analyzed in-game markerless motion capture and ball-tracking data from 3,958 swings by 247 NCAA Division I batters, examining hip–shoulder separation and bat speed both between and within batters; the published abstract reports that greater separation was associated with higher bat speed. Earlier, Sonnenfeld and colleagues used a markerless system to describe lead- and trail-hip motion during swings in 29 elite players, finding asymmetries between hips.

Read these precisely. The Hoechstetter study is a large retrospective observational analysis of in-game data: it shows an association, within and between batters, between a markerless-derived angle and a tracking-derived bat speed. It does not validate markerless swing kinematics against a laboratory reference, it does not show that increasing separation increases bat speed, and it says nothing about competitive outcomes. In searches completed for this course in November 2026 we found no peer-reviewed study comparing markerless and marker-based measurement of swing kinematics, wrist and forearm rotation, or bat orientation; at least one vendor has announced markerless bat-and-body tracking with validation figures reported in a press release, which is a vendor claim until its methods are published. Hitting creates specific difficulties for video models: the hands and bat move fastest, overlap each other and the body, and blur at ordinary frame rates.

Pose estimation infers joints from the visible body; multi-camera fitting produces 3D angles in the competitive task.

Not applicable to the measurement itself; no study shows that monitoring with either system improves performance.
Does the improvement transfer to competition?
In-game data are the competitive task, which is the main argument for them, provided the measurement is stable across stadiums and versions.

items: **(1) Biomechanical measurement:** Pitching: agreement studies exist and show offsets. Hitting: no peer-reviewed agreement study found.
**(2) Mechanics → mechanical output:** Pitching and hitting: in-game associations with velocity and bat speed are now published (weak to modest; observational).
**(3) Mechanics → competitive outcome:** We found no markerless study linking kinematics to competitive outcomes such as run value.
**(4) Demonstrated intervention effect:** No intervention trial using in-game markerless outcomes was found.
**(5) Retention and transfer:** Longitudinal in-game data could test retention and transfer; the published work is cross-sectional.

apply.text: For the synthetic pitcher, the defensible conclusion is that the 11° difference cannot be interpreted. The two systems are known to disagree in shoulder rotation; the published offsets for that variable are of the same order as the observed gap; and the setting changed at the same time as the instrument. To monitor him in games, establish a baseline with the in-game system across several starts and track change within that system. To relate in-game values to laboratory values, you would need simultaneous capture by both systems on the same pitches.

For a hitter, in-game markerless data can support descriptive questions — how consistent is the timing of pelvis rotation relative to stride across at-bats? — provided you estimate the system's within-hitter variability first. Do not treat wrist, forearm or bat-orientation outputs as validated, and keep tracking-derived bat metrics (bat speed, attack angle) conceptually separate from body kinematics.

A practical protocol for a club that wants to use in-game markerless data follows from this. First, choose a small set of variables with plausible relevance and decent published agreement — stride length and pelvis and trunk rotation timing before humeral rotation. Second, estimate each variable's within-athlete typical error from several outings in a stable period, by pitch type. Third, check stability across stadiums by comparing the same pitchers at home and away installations where possible. Fourth, record the software version with every value. Only then set flags for change, and set them per variable from its own error rather than from a generic percentage.

blocks.text: Midway through a season, your markerless vendor ships a new pose-estimation model and reports “improved accuracy.” Your trend lines for every pitcher shift by 3–6° on the update date. You cannot tell which values were closer to the truth, but you know the change is not physiological. Insist on version-stamped outputs, the ability to reprocess historical video with the new model, and a written description of what changed. A within-athlete monitoring system is only as stable as its software.

retain.text: Markerless capture moves biomechanics into the game by inferring joints from video, at the cost of system-specific offsets, weak long-axis rotations and dependence on a vendor's model. Pitching has agreement studies and in-game associations; hitting has in-game associations but, as of November 2026, no peer-reviewed agreement study that we could find. Track change within one system and version.

lessons.title: Force Plates, IMUs & EMG
lessons.summary: What ground reaction forces, inertial sensors and electromyography actually measure, how their signals are processed, and why a wearable 'elbow torque' is a model estimate rather than a measured load.
objectives: Derive impulse and centre of pressure from force-plate outputs and identify when each becomes unreliable.
Explain gyroscope drift, accelerometer gravity contamination, sensor fusion and saturation, and apply them to wearable throwing sensors.
Describe the EMG processing chain and state what EMG amplitude can and cannot tell you about muscle force.
lessons.executive: Force plates measure the force between foot and ground directly and well; their limits are installation (a pitching mound must be built around them) and the fact that they measure only the whole-body external force. Inertial sensors measure acceleration and rotation rate on the skin; orientation and position come from integration and fusion, which drift. A wearable elbow sensor does not measure ligament load: it combines arm kinematics with a body model to estimate a net joint moment, and its published comparison to motion capture found the estimate correlated but substantially lower. EMG shows when a muscle is electrically active, not how hard it pulls. None of these numbers is an injury probability.

explore.text: A synthetic right-handed pitcher wears an arm sensor for a bullpen session. His “elbow torque” averages 72 N·m on fastballs this week, against 66 N·m last week. The same week, force plates in the mound show his lead-leg peak vertical force rose from 1.9 to 2.1 body weights. A staff member proposes reducing his throwing volume because “his UCL load is up 9%.” All values are synthetic.
Which of the three numbers in this vignette is measured directly, which is estimated through a model, and which assumption would you test first?

The force-plate value is a direct measurement of the external force, subject to calibration and installation. The sensor's torque is a model output: it combines measured angular velocity and acceleration with assumed arm dimensions and mass properties to estimate a net moment at the elbow — the sum of everything that crosses the joint, not ligament tension. The claim that “UCL load is up 9%” adds two further inferences: that the net moment is borne by the ligament in a fixed proportion, and that a 9% change exceeds the sensor's measurement error. Neither has been shown.

understand.text: Force plates

A force plate measures three orthogonal force components and three moments about its own axes, using strain gauges or piezoelectric crystals at its supports. From these, the point of application of the resultant force on the surface — the centre of pressure (COP) — is computed. For a plate whose origin lies a distance h below its surface, the anteroposterior and mediolateral COP coordinates are obtained from the moments and the vertical force, for example x = (−My − h·Fx)/Fz and y = (Mx − h·Fy)/Fz in one common convention; sign conventions vary by manufacturer and must be checked. Ground reaction force and COP, combined with segment kinematics and inertial properties, are the inputs to inverse dynamics.

Two numbers worth computing. Impulse is the time integral of force, so a lead-leg braking force averaging 0.8 body weight for 0.10 s on a 90 kg pitcher (body weight ≈ 883 N) delivers an anteroposterior impulse of 0.8 × 883 × 0.10 ≈ 71 N·s, enough to change the body's forward momentum by 71 kg·m/s, or its centre-of-mass velocity by about 0.79 m/s. And because COP divides by Fz, when vertical force is small — at initial contact, or as the foot leaves the plate — tiny moment errors produce large COP excursions; laboratories therefore compute COP only above a force threshold.

Force–time curves carry more information than peaks. The rate of force development, the timing of the peak relative to foot contact and ball release, and the impulse in each direction describe how force is produced. In pitching, a mound with embedded plates is required for both legs; in hitting, two plates under the feet in the box allow each leg to be analyzed. Plates must be rigidly mounted, level, and of known natural frequency high enough that impacts do not excite plate vibration; mound installations with turf and clay over the plate change all three.
Inertial measurement units

An inertial measurement unit (IMU) combines a triaxial accelerometer, a triaxial gyroscope and often a magnetometer. The accelerometer measures specific force — linear acceleration minus gravity — in the sensor's own frame; the gyroscope measures angular velocity in that frame. Orientation is obtained by integrating angular velocity, and position by double integration of gravity-corrected acceleration. Both integrations accumulate error, so sensor-fusion algorithms (complementary or Kalman filters) correct orientation using gravity, and sometimes the magnetic field, as references. Camomilla and colleagues' systematic review of in-field sport applications found that most studies were conducted in training rather than competition and highlighted reliability and sensor-to-segment calibration as continuing concerns.

blocks.text: A gyroscope with an uncorrected bias of 0.5°/s accumulates 30° of orientation error per minute, because the error grows linearly with time. An accelerometer bias of 0.05 m/s², double-integrated over 2 s, gives a position error of ½ × 0.05 × 2² = 0.10 m, and the error grows with the square of time. Short, fast events such as a single throw are less affected than long recordings, which is why throwing sensors reset or re-reference between throws.

understand.text: Three additional IMU problems matter for baseball. Saturation: the throwing arm's angular velocities are among the fastest in sport, and a gyroscope whose range is lower than the peak clips the signal and corrupts every integrated quantity downstream, so check the datasheet range against the task. Sensor-to-segment alignment: the sensor measures its own axes, not the humerus's, so a calibration posture or functional movement is needed to relate them, and a strap that rotates on the arm changes the result. Magnetic disturbance: ferrous structures in stadiums and training facilities distort the magnetometer, so heading estimates indoors can be unreliable.
Wearable elbow-torque sensors

Boddy and colleagues compared a commercial arm sensor with marker-based motion capture during pitching. Arm slot and shoulder rotation correlated with motion-capture values and arm slot averaged about 8° lower; the sensor's “stress” metric correlated with motion-capture elbow varus torque but was about 41 N·m (39%) lower. Several authors were affiliated with a private training company. Camp and colleagues used the same type of sensor on 81 professional pitchers across about 82,000 throws and found within-pitcher relationships between estimated varus torque and arm slot, arm speed and shoulder rotation; that study described associations among sensor outputs and did not validate the sensor.

understand.title: Methodological note: what an inverse-dynamics elbow moment is

blocks.text: Inverse dynamics computes the net joint moment at the elbow as the moment required to produce the observed motion of the forearm–hand segment (and ball), given its mass, centre of mass and moments of inertia and the forces acting on it. The result is a net moment: the resultant of every muscle, ligament, capsule and bony contact force acting across the joint. It cannot partition load among structures. Its accuracy depends on joint-centre location, segment inertial parameters and filtering of the kinematics — the same issues covered in [Marker-Based Motion Capture](#b02-l1).

A single-IMU sensor on the forearm faces a harder problem: it measures one segment's motion and must model the rest, typically assuming segment lengths and masses from body height and mass. Its output is therefore an estimate of an estimate. That it tracks within-pitcher changes in the direction of a laboratory net moment is useful; that its absolute value is the ligament's load is not established and, by construction, cannot be.

understand.text: Electromyography

Electromyography records the electrical activity of muscle fibres. Surface electrodes over a muscle belly pick up a summed signal from many motor units and are susceptible to crosstalk from neighbouring muscles; fine-wire electrodes inserted into a muscle record more selectively, including deep muscles such as the subscapularis, but are invasive and sample a small volume. The European SENIAM project, summarized by Hermens and colleagues from a review of 144 papers, produced recommendations for sensor construction and placement for 27 muscles.

Processing typically involves band-pass filtering to remove movement artifact and high-frequency noise, full-wave rectification, and low-pass filtering to obtain a linear envelope (or computing a moving root-mean-square). Because raw amplitude depends on electrode placement, skin impedance and subcutaneous tissue, amplitudes are normalized — commonly to a maximal voluntary isometric contraction or to the peak within the task — before comparison across muscles or people.

challenge.text: EMG amplitude is not muscle force. The relationship between EMG and force is reasonably monotonic only in isometric conditions for a given muscle; in dynamic movements muscle length and shortening velocity change force for the same activation, the electrode moves relative to the muscle, and the electromechanical delay separates electrical onset from force production. In throwing and swinging, EMG is best read for timing and relative activity patterns, not as a dynamometer.

Force plates have their own boundary conditions. A plate measures only the force at its surface: on a mound, the clay, turf and slope between foot and plate alter both the measured force and its point of application, and a front foot that lands partly off the plate produces a plausible but incomplete curve. Plates also report the whole-body external force, the sum of every segment's mass times acceleration plus weight, and cannot say which segment produced it. Statements such as “the lead leg transferred force into the trunk” require inverse dynamics or energy analysis, with the assumptions those methods carry.

Normalization choices can reverse a conclusion. Normalizing to a maximal isometric contraction can yield values above 100% in ballistic tasks; normalizing to the task's own peak removes information about overall intensity. When two studies disagree about which muscle is “more active” during arm cocking, check first whether they normalized the same way.

Wearable sensors deserve particular scrutiny because they generate large datasets cheaply. A large number of throws does not fix a biased instrument; it estimates the bias precisely. The question for any wearable is the size of its bias and limits of agreement against a reference for the variable you will use, and its within-athlete typical error in the setting where you will use it.

challenge.caption: Applying the standard to: “A wearable sensor's elbow torque tracks UCL load and can guide throwing workload.”
rows: Sensor torque correlates with laboratory net elbow varus moment but reads substantially lower; within-pitcher relationships with arm slot and arm speed have been described.
Kinematics of one segment plus a body model produce an estimated net joint moment.
Boddy et al. 2019 (comparison, company-affiliated); Camp et al. 2017 (association across many throws).
The share of the net moment borne by the ligament; within-pitcher typical error in games; tissue capacity, which is not measured at all.
Has changing the variable improved performance?
No evidence was reviewed that sensor-guided workload decisions improve performance.
Does the improvement transfer to competition?
Not applicable to performance; the claim concerns health monitoring.
What are the implications for loading or potential injury-related risk?
A net joint moment is a mechanical load estimate, not a ligament load and not an injury probability; injury decisions belong to medical staff.

items: **(1) Biomechanical measurement:** The sensor measures arm kinematics directly and estimates net moment through a model with known bias.
**(2) Mechanics → mechanical output:** Within-pitcher associations between estimated torque and arm speed are reported.
**(3) Mechanics → competitive outcome:** No link from sensor torque to competitive outcome is reviewed here.
**(4) Demonstrated intervention effect:** No trial shows that managing throwing by sensor torque changes outcomes.
**(5) Retention and transfer:** Not studied for retention or transfer.

apply.text: Return to the vignette. The 6 N·m increase in estimated torque coincided with a rise in lead-leg force, which suggests the pitcher threw harder; higher arm speed is associated with higher estimated torque in Camp et al. Before any decision, ask for the sensor's within-pitcher typical error from repeated sessions, confirm the strap position and sensor firmware were unchanged, and check velocity. The appropriate output to the medical and performance staff is a description — “estimated net elbow moment increased by an amount near the measurement error while velocity rose” — not “UCL load is up 9%.” Workload decisions remain clinical and multidisciplinary.

For hitters, force plates under each foot and IMUs on the bat and lead forearm are the practical field kit. Bat-mounted sensors measure the bat's own motion, a rigid body with known geometry, which is a friendlier problem than estimating joint angles from skin-mounted sensors. Their bat-speed definitions differ from tracking definitions, so values from a sensor and from stadium tracking should not be compared directly.

apply.title: Executive twist: the medical staff asks for one number

blocks.text: The medical staff wants a single daily “arm load” number per pitcher. Any number you provide will be treated as a measurement of tissue stress. Offer instead a short panel: throws, velocity, estimated net moment with its measurement error, and a flag only when change exceeds that error. State in writing that the sensor estimates a net joint moment and does not measure ligament load or injury risk.

State what each number is before discussing what it means.

A gyroscope bias of 0.2°/s is uncorrected for 90 s. How much orientation error accumulates?

IMU orientation and position come from integration and fusion and drift without references; saturation corrupts fast-arm data.

EMG amplitude reflects electrical activity; normalization choices and dynamic conditions prevent reading it as force.
A joint moment, measured or estimated, is not an injury probability.

lessons.title: Video, Ball Tracking & Bat Tracking
lessons.summary: How frame rate, exposure and camera geometry limit what video can resolve, what stadium ball- and bat-tracking metrics are defined to mean, and why tracking outputs are not a biomechanical assessment.
objectives: Calculate the temporal and angular resolution of video for fast pitching and hitting events.
Quantify perspective error in 2D analysis and explain when 3D reconstruction is required.
State the published definitions of tracking-derived bat metrics and distinguish them from body kinematics, including synchronization requirements for integrating systems.
lessons.executive: Video is limited by time and geometry. At 240 frames per second, a shoulder rotating at 7,000°/s moves about 29° between frames, and a millisecond-scale bat–ball contact usually falls between frames entirely. A single camera sees angles projected onto its image plane, so a 45° segment can read 49° or more when the plane of motion is rotated. Stadium tracking systems such as Hawk-Eye produce precise outputs about the ball and the bat — bat speed at the sweet spot, swing length, attack angle — but these describe the implement, not the body that produced it. They are mechanical outputs; they are not a biomechanical assessment.

explore.text: A hitting coach films a synthetic hitter at 240 frames per second from the open side and reports that the bat “was level through contact” and that the hitter's lead elbow “extended at 30° before contact.” The stadium bat-tracking output for the same swing reports an attack angle of 14°. Values are synthetic.
Before reading on: at 240 frames per second, how far does a bat sweet spot moving at 32 m/s travel between consecutive frames? Could the coach have seen contact?

The interval between frames is 1/240 s ≈ 4.17 ms. The sweet spot travels 32 × 0.00417 ≈ 0.13 m — about five inches — between frames. If bat–ball contact lasts on the order of a millisecond (take 1 ms as a working value), the chance that any given frame falls within contact is about 1/4.17 ≈ 0.24. Most 240 Hz swings have no frame at contact; “through contact” is an interpolation. And an elbow angle read from one camera depends on the camera's position, as the next section shows.

understand.text: Temporal resolution

Sampling theory requires a sampling rate of at least twice the highest frequency present in the signal to avoid aliasing; in practice biomechanists sample several times higher than the frequencies of interest so that peaks and event timing are resolved. Each frame is also an exposure of finite duration: a short shutter limits motion blur, at the cost of light.

understand.caption: What different frame rates resolve for fast baseball events (working values)
headers: Expected frames during a 1 ms contact
understand.note: Arithmetic on working values chosen for illustration: 7,000°/s as an order-of-magnitude shoulder internal-rotation peak, 32 m/s as a bat sweet-spot speed and 1 ms as a contact duration. Not measured data.

understand.text: Two consequences follow for peaks and timing. A sampled peak is the largest sample, not the largest value; with 29° between samples, the true peak can lie anywhere between frames, and smoothing reduces it further. Event timing — foot contact, maximum external rotation, release, contact — is uncertain by up to half a frame interval either side, about ±2 ms at 240 Hz. Sequencing claims built on differences of a few milliseconds between segment peaks need either higher sampling or explicit uncertainty.

Exposure is the second constraint. A frame exposed for 1/1,000 s while a ball travels at 40 m/s smears the ball over 40 mm, more than half its diameter; the hand at release, moving at a comparable speed, blurs similarly. Pose models and human coders then locate a blurred hand or bat less precisely. Shortening exposure to 1/4,000 s reduces the smear to 10 mm but needs four times the light, which is why high-speed capture outdoors at night or in a dim cage often trades frame rate or exposure for image quality.

Interpolating between frames recovers some lost information when the movement is smooth, but not when it is not. A smooth trunk rotation can be fitted between samples well; the instant of bat–ball contact, a discontinuity in the ball's velocity, cannot be reconstructed from frames on either side unless you model the collision itself. Tracking systems therefore estimate contact from trajectories of ball and bat before and after the event rather than from an image of it.
Geometry: 2D versus 3D

A single camera projects the world onto its image plane. Consider a segment inclined 45° above horizontal in a plane rotated 30° away from the camera's image plane about the vertical axis. Its horizontal extent appears shortened by cos 30° ≈ 0.866, its vertical extent is unchanged, and its apparent inclination becomes atan(tan 45° / cos 30°) = atan(1.155) ≈ 49.1°. Rotate the plane 60° away and the same segment appears at atan(2) ≈ 63.4°. Lens distortion and the athlete moving toward or away from the camera add further error.

blocks.text: Two-dimensional analysis is valid only for motion that stays in a plane parallel to the image plane, with the camera far enough away and perpendicular to that plane, and with the scale known in that plane. Pitching and hitting are three-dimensional rotations: trunk rotation, shoulder rotation and bat path are all out of any single plane. Two-dimensional video is excellent for timing qualitative events, counting, and communication with athletes; it is not a measurement of joint angles in throwing or swinging. Three-dimensional reconstruction requires at least two calibrated, synchronized views of each point of interest.

understand.text: Stadium ball and bat tracking

Major League Baseball's Statcast system has used Hawk-Eye optical tracking since 2020, with twelve cameras around each park for pitch, batted-ball and player tracking and a pose-tracking capability that follows players' body positions. MLB's 2020 description listed 100 frames per second for the cameras dedicated to pitch tracking; later press coverage of bat tracking described higher frame rates that we could not confirm from a primary MLB source.

Statcast's bat-tracking glossary defines bat speed as the speed of the bat's sweet spot at the point of contact, or where contact would have occurred on a miss; a player's average is computed from the faster portion of his swings. Swing length is the total distance in feet travelled by the head of the bat in three dimensions from the start of tracking until impact. Attack angle is the vertical direction in which the sweet spot is travelling at contact. These are defined properties of the bat's motion, computed from tracked bat positions.

Ball-tracking release measurements — release height, side, extension, velocity, spin rate and axis — are similarly properties of the ball at or after release, reconstructed from the trajectory. Extension, for instance, is a ball position, not a measure of stride length or trunk posture, though both influence it.

understand.title: Methodological note: synchronizing and integrating systems

blocks.text: Combining instruments — force plates at 1,000 Hz, marker cameras at 240 Hz, a radar or tracking system, EMG at 2,000 Hz — requires a common time base. Hardware synchronization uses a shared trigger or clock; software synchronization aligns timestamps or detected events after the fact. Data at different rates are resampled to a common rate, and filters must be matched before signals are combined in inverse dynamics.

The size of a synchronization error is easy to compute. An offset of one 240 Hz frame (4.17 ms) between force and motion data, when the bat is moving at 32 m/s, places the bat about 0.13 m from where it was when the force was recorded; at foot contact, it shifts the onset of ground force relative to the stride by the same interval. Pairing a tracking system's contact time with a markerless system's swing frames inherits both systems' clocks and both systems' event definitions. Every integrated report should state how synchronization was achieved and verified.

Tracking outputs and body kinematics also come with different definitions of the same event. “Contact” in bat tracking is a modelled bat–ball intersection; “ball release” in markerless pitching is often a detected instant from hand–ball separation in video. Studies that combine them — for example, Hoechstetter et al.'s analysis pairing in-game markerless kinematics with ball-tracking data — must align these events; check how.

challenge.text: The central error in applied practice is treating tracking outputs as biomechanics. Bat speed, attack angle and swing length tell you what the bat did. They do not tell you how the body produced it, what the joints experienced, or which of many movement solutions the hitter used. Two hitters with identical bat speed can differ greatly in pelvis–trunk timing, and one hitter can produce the same attack angle with different body postures in different pitch locations. Release metrics similarly describe the ball, not the arm.

Definitions also embed choices that affect interpretation. Average bat speed computed from the faster swings excludes checked and defensive swings, which is sensible for estimating capacity but means the average is not a mean of all swings. Attack angle is read at the contact point, and the bat's arc through the zone means that contact at a different pitch height or depth can change the angle, so a change in attack angle can reflect pitch location rather than a change in swing. Changes in the tracking system or its algorithms can shift league-wide distributions. Statcast's definitions are published, but their measurement error for an individual swing is not, to our knowledge, documented in a peer-reviewed validation.

Body pose tracked by a stadium system raises the same questions as any markerless system, plus two of its own. The cameras were placed for ball tracking and broadcast-scale coverage, not for joint-level biomechanics, so occlusion and viewing angles for the throwing arm or the hitter's hands may be unfavourable. And the pose outputs available to clubs may be produced at a lower rate, or with a different skeletal model, from the ball tracking. Aguinaldo and colleagues' comparison is the only peer-reviewed evaluation we found of an in-stadium Hawk-Eye installation for pitching biomechanics; it found joint position errors of the order of 5–6 cm and the weakest agreement for shoulder rotation.

challenge.caption: Applying the standard to: “Raising a hitter's tracked bat speed by 2 mph will improve his results.”
rows: Bat speed is a tracked property of the bat at contact; harder-hit balls require faster bats, other things being equal.
Momentum transfer at collision: higher bat speed at the sweet spot raises potential exit velocity, if contact quality is maintained.
Collision physics supports the mechanical relationship; tracking data describe distributions of bat speed among hitters.
Whether a training-induced increase preserves contact rate, timing and pitch selection; the individual-swing measurement error of the tracking system.
Has changing the variable improved performance?
Not established here: whether interventions that raise bat speed improve competitive results for a given hitter.
Does the improvement transfer to competition?
Unknown without a game-based evaluation over sufficient plate appearances.
What are the implications for loading or potential injury-related risk?
Faster swings and heavier training implements may change loading; no inference about injury is supported by tracking data.

items: **(1) Biomechanical measurement:** Bat speed is a well-defined tracking output; its per-swing error is not documented in the peer-reviewed literature we reviewed.
**(2) Mechanics → mechanical output:** Higher bat speed raises potential exit velocity through collision physics (Week 7 develops this).
**(3) Mechanics → competitive outcome:** Relationships between bat speed and outcomes depend on contact, timing and decisions; they are not established for individuals by tracking alone.
**(4) Demonstrated intervention effect:** Intervention evidence for bat-speed training and its effect on game results is not reviewed this week.
**(5) Retention and transfer:** Retention and transfer require repeated in-game measurement over time.

apply.text: Rewrite the coach's report. “Level through contact” cannot be observed at 240 Hz from one side and conflicts with a tracked attack angle of 14°; the tracked value is the better estimate of bat direction at contact, subject to the system's unknown per-swing error, and it should be read against the pitch's location. The elbow angle should be described as a 2D projected angle from a stated camera position, used for qualitative comparison between swings filmed identically, not as a joint measurement.

For a pitcher, combine instruments by question. Release consistency across a season: ball-tracking release data. Arm path timing within the delivery: high-speed video at 480 Hz or more from fixed, documented positions, or markerless capture. Joint angles and moments: 3D capture with synchronized force plates in a laboratory. A report that mixes these should label each number with its instrument.
