lessons.title: Reliability, Validity & Measurement Error
lessons.summary: The statistics that decide whether a biomechanical number can support a decision: typical error, ICC forms, Bland–Altman limits of agreement, minimal detectable change, and within-athlete variability, worked through with real arithmetic.
objectives: Distinguish accuracy from precision and reliability from validity, and match each to the statistic that estimates it.
Calculate typical error, ICC, limits of agreement and MDC95 from trial or session data.
Judge whether an observed change in an athlete exceeds measurement error and biological variability for a specific decision.
lessons.executive: Every biomechanical number has an error band, and decisions about individual athletes live inside it. Typical error is the standard deviation of an athlete's repeated measurements; from it, the minimal detectable change at 95% confidence is about 2.77 times the typical error. ICC is a ratio of between-athlete to total variance, so it is high in heterogeneous samples and says little about whether one athlete changed. Bland–Altman bias and limits of agreement tell you whether two systems can be swapped; correlation cannot. Before acting on a mechanical change, require that it exceed the MDC from the same system, and that the comparison not cross systems.

explore.text: A synthetic pitcher's peak shoulder external rotation is 177° (mean of 10 fastballs) in a laboratory session in January. After a six-week mobility and drill block he measures 171° in the same laboratory. A second analyst points out that his March in-game markerless value is 166°. The development staff want to know whether the drill block reduced his layback, and by how much.
Write down what you would need to know to answer — about the instrument, about the athlete's normal variation, and about the comparison — before you calculate anything.

You need four things: the laboratory's session-to-session typical error for this variable in pitchers like him; his own trial-to-trial variability within a session; the bias between the laboratory and the in-game system; and whether the change matters for any decision. This lesson builds each from data.

understand.text: Four distinctions

understand.title: Prerequisite: variance, standard deviation and why errors add in quadrature

blocks.text: The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, the average squared deviation from the mean. When two independent sources of error combine, their variances add, not their standard deviations: a change score built from two measurements, each with error SD σ, has variance 2σ² and SD √2·σ. Likewise, a measured value that contains independent biological variation (SD 2.5°) and instrument error (SD 1.5°) has total SD √(2.5² + 1.5²) ≈ 2.9°, not 4.0°. Averaging k independent trials divides the variance by k and the SD by √k. These three rules generate every formula in this lesson.

The 1.96 multiplier comes from the normal distribution: 95% of values from a normal distribution lie within 1.96 standard deviations of its mean. Using it assumes errors are roughly normal and unrelated to the size of the measurement; when that fails, a transformation or a nonparametric interval is needed.

understand.text: **Accuracy** is closeness to the true value; **precision** is closeness of repeated measurements to one another. **Validity** asks whether an instrument measures what it claims, usually assessed against a reference; **reliability** asks whether it gives consistent results on repetition. Hopkins identifies three components of reliability: within-subject random variation (the typical error), systematic change in the mean between trials, and the retest correlation. Atkinson and Nevill emphasize that the choice of statistic should follow from how the measurement will be used, and that relative indices such as correlations must be complemented by absolute indices in the units of measurement.

understand.caption: Accuracy and precision are independent
cells: Scattered and offset: useless for individuals and groups.
Tight but offset: good for tracking change within the system; wrong absolute values (typical of a system-specific bias).
Scattered around the truth: group means are fine, individual values are not.
Tight and centred: the goal, rarely achieved for long-axis joint rotations.
understand.note: A markerless system with a constant offset from the marker system sits in the lower-right cell for within-system monitoring and the upper-left problem disappears only if you never mix systems.

understand.text: Typical error and the minimal detectable change

In a two-session test–retest design, the typical error (TE) equals the standard deviation of the difference scores divided by √2, because each difference contains the error of two measurements. To decide whether an individual's change exceeds error at 95% confidence, the change score's error (√2 × TE) is multiplied by 1.96, giving the minimal detectable change MDC95 = 1.96 × √2 × TE ≈ 2.77 × TE. Weir derives the same quantity from the standard error of measurement.

understand.caption: Synthetic test–retest data: peak shoulder external rotation (°), laboratory marker-based system, eight pitchers, sessions one week apart; each value is a mean of ten fastballs
understand.note: Synthetic data constructed for teaching. Mean difference 1.375°; SD of differences 2.615°.

understand.text: Work it through. The mean difference is 1.38°, a small systematic shift (perhaps a learning or warm-up effect). The standard deviation of the eight differences is 2.62°. Typical error = 2.62 / √2 = 1.85°. MDC95 = 1.96 × √2 × 1.85 = 5.13°. A single pitcher's session-to-session change must exceed about 5° before you can be 95% confident it is not error. Note what this typical error contains: because each session value is a session mean, it includes day-to-day biological variation as well as instrument error, which is appropriate when the decision concerns change across days.
ICC: what it measures, and its forms

The intraclass correlation coefficient expresses reliability as the proportion of total variance that lies between subjects. Koo and Li describe ten forms defined by three choices — the model (one-way random, two-way random, two-way mixed), the type (single measurement or mean of k measurements) and the definition (absolute agreement or consistency) — and recommend reporting all three with confidence intervals, interpreting the lower confidence bound: below 0.5 poor, 0.5–0.75 moderate, 0.75–0.9 good, above 0.9 excellent.

For the eight pitchers above, a two-way ANOVA gives a between-pitcher mean square of 98.71, a between-session mean square of 7.56 and an error mean square of 3.42. ICC(3,1), consistency, single measure = (98.71 − 3.42) / (98.71 + 3.42) = 0.93. ICC(2,1), absolute agreement, single measure = (98.71 − 3.42) / (98.71 + 3.42 + 2 × (7.56 − 3.42) / 8) = 0.92; the small systematic shift lowers absolute agreement slightly. The square root of the error mean square, 1.85°, equals the typical error computed from the differences.

understand.title: Methodological note: why ICC can mislead about individuals

blocks.text: ICC ≈ σ²between / (σ²between + σ²error). Hold the error constant at TE = 1.85° (σ²error = 3.42). In a heterogeneous sample whose true between-pitcher SD is 6.7°, ICC ≈ 44.9 / (44.9 + 3.42) ≈ 0.93. In a homogeneous group — pitchers selected for similar layback, SD 2.5° — ICC ≈ 6.25 / (6.25 + 3.42) ≈ 0.65. The instrument is identical and the MDC is identical; only the sample changed. ICC answers “can this measure rank athletes in this population?” The typical error and MDC answer “can it detect change in one athlete?” Report both.

understand.text: Agreement between systems: Bland–Altman

Bland and Altman argued that correlation is inappropriate for comparing two measurement methods, because two methods can be highly correlated while disagreeing substantially. Their method plots each pair's difference against its mean and reports the mean difference (bias) and the 95% limits of agreement, bias ± 1.96 × SD of the differences, with a check for whether the difference changes with magnitude.

understand.caption: Synthetic paired data: the same pitches captured simultaneously by a laboratory marker-based system and a field markerless system, peak shoulder external rotation (°)
understand.note: Synthetic data. Bias −7.88°; SD of differences 2.17°; limits of agreement −12.12° to −3.63°.

understand.text: The field system reads 7.9° lower on average. The limits of agreement are −7.88 ± 1.96 × 2.17, from −12.1° to −3.6°: for an individual pitch, the field value is expected to be between about 4° and 12° below the laboratory value. Correlation between the two columns is high (the rankings agree), which is exactly the situation Bland and Altman warned about. Looking at the last column, the largest differences occur at the largest means, a hint of proportional bias that a larger sample should test.

Bland and Altman also stressed two refinements that validation reports often omit. The bias is an estimate with its own confidence interval, which with eight pairs is wide; and when the differences grow with the magnitude of the measurement — proportional bias — a single pair of limits misrepresents agreement at both ends of the range, so differences should be modelled against the mean or analyzed on a transformed scale.

challenge.text: Within-athlete variability is not noise to be averaged away; it is part of the athlete. The same synthetic pitcher's ten fastballs in one session produce peak external rotation values of 176, 179, 174, 178, 181, 175, 177, 180, 173 and 177°: mean 177.0°, SD 2.58°. The standard error of the ten-pitch mean is 2.58 / √10 = 0.82°, so the session mean is estimated precisely, but any single pitch can sit 4–5° from it. Comparing one pitch before with one pitch after a drill block conflates pitch-to-pitch variation with change. Averaging trials reduces the random component of error by √k only if trial errors are independent; it does not touch bias, and it does not remove real day-to-day variation.

Whether a value that exceeds the MDC is meaningful remains a separate question. MDC addresses statistical detectability; it says nothing about whether the change matters. Atkinson and Nevill argue that acceptable measurement error should be judged against an analytical goal set by the intended use; sports-science practice often expresses that goal as a smallest worthwhile change tied to performance. For most biomechanical variables, however, no such anchor exists, because the variable's relationship to performance or health for an individual is not established. Lerch and colleagues' finding that within-pitcher variability was similar across in-game and laboratory settings for most variables, alongside large differences in means, shows why both random and systematic components must be estimated in the setting of use.
Measurement uncertainty and fitness for purpose

Measurement uncertainty is the honest statement of the range within which the true value plausibly lies, combining every known component: random error, residual bias after any correction, the uncertainty of the correction itself, and biological variability if the target is the athlete's usual value rather than one pitch. For the opening pitcher, a laboratory session mean of 171° carries a within-session standard error of about 0.8° from pitch-to-pitch variation, but a day-to-day typical error of 1.85° if the question is his usual layback this month. Which uncertainty applies depends on the question.

items: **Name the decision.** What will you do differently depending on the number, and what size of change would alter that action?
**Match the error to the decision.** Use the typical error from the same system, setting, athlete population and variable; require MDC smaller than the change that matters.
**Keep comparisons within one system and version,** or apply a correction only with the uncertainty of the correction stated.
**Decide how many trials to average,** given that averaging reduces random error and pitch-to-pitch variability but not bias or genuine day-to-day change.
**Re-estimate error periodically,** because hardware, software, installation and athletes change.

challenge.text: Atkinson and Nevill frame this as setting an analytical goal before collecting reliability data: an instrument is not reliable or unreliable in the abstract, but adequate or inadequate for detecting a change of a specified size in a specified use. Weir makes the same point in practice by deriving the minimal difference from the SEM rather than relying on an ICC threshold.

challenge.caption: Applying the standard to: “A 6° decrease in peak shoulder external rotation after a drill block shows the drill worked.”
rows: Laboratory session mean fell from 177° to 171°, a change of 6°.
The drill changed arm-cocking mechanics, reducing layback.
The change exceeds this laboratory's MDC95 of 5.1°, so it is probably not measurement error alone.
Whether reduced layback was the goal; whether it reflects the drill, fatigue, mobility or season timing; whether it persists. No control condition.
Has changing the variable improved performance?
Not shown: no velocity, command or other performance change is reported, and a mechanical change is not an improvement by itself.
Does the improvement transfer to competition?
Not tested: retention after the drill ends, and in-game values from the same system.
What are the implications for loading or potential injury-related risk?
Less external rotation is not, by itself, lower injury risk; any loading interpretation requires kinetics and clinical input.

items: **(1) Biomechanical measurement:** A 6° change exceeds the same-system MDC95 (5.1°); comparing with the in-game value would cross systems with a −7.9° bias.
**(2) Mechanics → mechanical output:** Whether layback is related to velocity for this pitcher is not established by this measurement.
**(3) Mechanics → competitive outcome:** No competitive outcome is involved.
**(4) Demonstrated intervention effect:** A single pre–post change without a control cannot attribute cause to the drill.
**(5) Retention and transfer:** Retention and transfer require a delayed retest and in-game data from one system.

apply.text: Answer the opening question. Laboratory to laboratory, 177° to 171° is a 6° change, just beyond the MDC95 of 5.1°: probably real, modestly so, with a single-pitcher pre–post design that cannot attribute it to the drill. The March in-game value of 166° cannot be compared with either laboratory value without correcting for the system bias; using the synthetic agreement data, 166° in the field corresponds to a laboratory value of roughly 166 + 7.9 ≈ 174°, with an individual-level uncertainty spanning the limits of agreement (about 170°–178°). The in-game number offers no evidence of a further decrease. The right report says: “Probable decrease of about 6° in the laboratory; cause not established; in-game value not comparable without correction; retest in the laboratory in four weeks and establish an in-game baseline.”

For hitters, the same arithmetic applies to tracked bat speed. If a hitter's game-to-game typical error in average bat speed is, say, 0.9 mph (a synthetic value), the MDC95 is 2.5 mph; a 1.5 mph increase after an off-season program is not yet distinguishable from variation. Measure the typical error from your own data before you set targets.

blocks.text: An analyst proposes coloring a pitcher's dashboard tile red whenever a mechanical variable changes by more than 5% from his baseline. For a variable near 175°, 5% is 8.8°, larger than the MDC; for a variable near 20°, 5% is 1°, far smaller than any plausible error. Percent thresholds applied uniformly guarantee false alarms on some variables and missed changes on others. Set each variable's threshold from its own typical error in the system and setting where it is collected, and document it beside the tile.

retain.text: Accuracy is about bias, precision about random error; validity needs a reference, reliability needs repetition. Typical error and MDC answer individual questions; ICC answers ranking questions in a particular sample; Bland–Altman answers interchangeability. A change matters only if it exceeds error in the same system and connects to a decision.
Compute MDC95 for a typical error of 2.4°.
Why can a measure have an ICC of 0.95 and still be unable to detect a 4° change in one athlete?
What two numbers from a Bland–Altman analysis would you need before comparing an athlete's laboratory and in-game values?

takeaways: Typical error = SD of test–retest differences / √2; MDC95 = 1.96 × √2 × TE ≈ 2.77 × TE.
ICC depends on sample heterogeneity and must be reported with its model, type, definition and confidence interval.
Bland–Altman bias and limits of agreement, not correlation, decide whether two systems are interchangeable.
Within-athlete variability is real; averaging trials shrinks random error but not bias.
A statistically detectable change is not automatically a meaningful or beneficial one.

check.prompt: Test–retest differences for a variable have a standard deviation of 3.4°. What is the typical error?
check.explanation: Each difference contains the error of two measurements, so its variance is twice the single-measurement error variance; dividing the SD by √2 recovers the typical error of one measurement.

check.prompt: Two systems' peak elbow flexion values correlate at r = 0.96 across 40 pitchers. What can you conclude about interchangeability?

options.text: The systems are interchangeable because the correlation is very high.
Nothing yet: correlation can be high despite a large bias or wide limits of agreement.
The systems disagree, because r is below 1.
The newer system is valid.

check.explanation: Bland and Altman showed that correlation measures association, not agreement. One system could read 10° higher on every pitch and still correlate almost perfectly. Interchangeability requires bias and limits of agreement in the units of measurement.

optionFeedback.a: High correlation is compatible with a large constant or proportional bias.
optionFeedback.c: Some disagreement is expected; the question is whether bias and limits are small enough for the decision.
optionFeedback.d: Agreement with another imperfect system does not establish validity.

check.prompt: The same instrument and protocol produce ICC = 0.93 in one sample and ICC = 0.65 in another. The typical error is identical. The most likely explanation is…

options.text: the second sample's athletes are more homogeneous
the second sample was measured less accurately
the ICC form differed between samples
the second sample was larger

check.explanation: ICC is the ratio of between-subject variance to total variance. With the same error variance, a more homogeneous sample has less between-subject variance and therefore a lower ICC, though the ability to detect change in an individual (MDC) is unchanged.

optionFeedback.b: The typical error is identical, so measurement precision did not change.
optionFeedback.c: Different forms can change ICC, but the stem holds the protocol constant; heterogeneity explains this pattern directly.
optionFeedback.d: Sample size changes the precision of the ICC estimate, not its expected value.

exercise.title: The Measurement Science Laboratory

intro.text: Two fictional systems measure the same synthetic right-handed pitcher: a laboratory marker-based system and a field markerless system. You control four quantities — the field system's systematic bias, each system's random error, the pitcher's within-athlete (pitch-to-pitch and day-to-day) variability, and a true change in his mechanics between two test occasions. The laboratory then generates trials and shows synchronized shoulder and trunk traces from both systems, joint-angle comparisons pitch by pitch, a Bland–Altman plot with bias and limits of agreement, typical error, ICC and MDC95.

For each scenario, record your judgement — real change, not distinguishable from error, or not comparable — before revealing the true value.

debrief.text: The laboratory shows three things. First, a constant bias is invisible within one system and decisive across systems: if baseline and follow-up come from different instruments, a bias of a few degrees manufactures or hides change. Second, the minimal detectable change depends on random error and within-athlete variability in the setting of use, not on the ICC, which also responds to how different the athletes are from one another. Third, averaging pitches shrinks random variation by roughly the square root of the number of trials, but it never removes bias.

It does not show which system is closer to the truth: both are simulated against a known true value that real data never provide. It does not tell you whether a real change in layback matters for performance or health — that requires the evidence tiers you applied in each lesson. And its error model is simpler than reality: real errors can be proportional to magnitude, differ between pitch types, and change when software is updated.

assumptions: All athlete data are synthetic and generated from a known true value; no real athlete, system or club is represented.
Random errors are normally distributed, independent between trials and constant across the measurement range unless proportional bias is switched on.
System bias is constant for a given setting; within-athlete variability is shared by both systems because they measure the same pitches.
MDC95 is computed as 1.96 × √2 × typical error; limits of agreement as bias ± 1.96 × SD of paired differences; ICC as a two-way model, single measurement.
The fictional systems are not models of any commercial product.

case.title: Validated Against What? Critiquing a Markerless Pitching Study
case.fiction: The study summarized is real and cited from verified records. The club, its people, the vendor's deck and all numbers in the exhibit are fictional or synthetic.

body.text: This case asks you to critique a real, peer-reviewed validation study. The study is summarized in our own words from its published abstract and verified bibliographic records; the decision context — a development department at a fictional professional club, its people and its data — is invented.

Dana Okafor, director of pitching development for the fictional Northfield club, has been asked whether the club can stop sending pitchers to an external marker-based laboratory each winter and rely instead on a markerless system installed in its spring-training complex and, eventually, in affiliate stadiums. The vendor's sales deck cites a peer-reviewed study and describes the markerless system as “validated against the gold standard.” The club's biomechanist, Luis Ferreira, has been asked to brief the department on what that study actually establishes. Okafor wants a recommendation in two weeks; the external laboratory's winter booking deadline falls in three.

Ferreira's first observation is that “validated” is not a property of a system. A study validates particular variables, measured in particular conditions, against a particular reference, for a particular purpose. His briefing therefore begins with the study itself.

Fleisig and colleagues, at a long-established pitching biomechanics laboratory, set out to compare pitching kinematics measured with a markerless and a marker-based system. Thirty pitchers, with a mean age of about 17 years, threw fastballs while both systems recorded simultaneously: a nine-camera markerless system and a twelve-camera marker-based system, both sampling at 240 Hz. In all, 275 fastballs were analyzed. Because the same pitches were recorded by both systems at the same time, differences between the systems cannot be explained by the athlete throwing differently.

For the time-series variables analyzed, agreement between the two systems' waveforms was high, with coefficients of multiple correlation from 0.88 to 0.97: the movement patterns rose and fell together through the delivery. Discrete values, however, differed systematically between systems for several kinematic parameters. The authors concluded that the two systems produced similar patterns but that, given the differences, a separate database of normative ranges should be established for each system.

Ferreira notes what the abstract-level record does and does not let him say. He can say how many pitchers and pitches were analyzed, how the systems were configured, the range of waveform agreement and the authors' recommendation. He should not quote specific variable-by-variable differences unless he reads them from the full paper, and he should not assume which commercial markerless product was used unless the paper names it. The vendor's deck implies that this study validated its current software; Ferreira cannot confirm that the system, model version or camera layout match.
What the department is tempted to conclude

Three readings circulate in the department before the briefing. Okafor's assistant reads the CMC values as proof that the systems are interchangeable. A pitching coach, Marisol Reyes, reads the recommendation of separate norms as proof that the markerless system is inaccurate. A data analyst, Priya Nair, reads the study as irrelevant, because the club wants in-game measurement and the study was done in a laboratory with adolescents.

Each reading takes one feature of the study and stretches it. High CMC shows similar shapes, not equal values; separate norms acknowledge systematic differences between two imperfect systems, not which one is closer to the bone; and a laboratory study of younger pitchers is exactly where a concurrent comparison must start, even if it cannot settle the in-game question.

Ferreira's briefing also places the study among later work. Aguinaldo and colleagues recorded 18 collegiate pitchers simultaneously with a marker-based reference, an in-stadium system and a portable markerless system, reporting mean per-joint position errors of roughly 52–57 mm, the best agreement for stride length and the least for shoulder rotation. Lerch and colleagues compared within-pitcher variability between laboratory marker-based and in-game markerless data, finding it similar for most variables but larger in-game for maximum shoulder external rotation and elbow flexion at that instant, and noting large differences in means; different pitchers were measured in each setting.
For hitting, Ferreira found no peer-reviewed agreement study of markerless swing kinematics. That matters because the club also wants to use the system for hitters.

The external laboratory offers continuity: five winters of data on many of the club's pitchers, processed with one model. The markerless system offers scale, in-game data and lower cost per athlete. Switching would break every pitcher's longitudinal series, because a marker-based baseline cannot be compared with a markerless follow-up without a correction that applies at the group level, not reliably to individuals. Running both for a year would cost more but would generate the club's own agreement data on its own athletes. Reyes worries that coaches will see markerless shoulder values several degrees different from the laboratory values they know and lose trust; Nair worries that waiting a year means another season without in-game data.
Okafor asks Ferreira for three things: a fair summary of what the study shows, a list of what it does not show, and a recommendation that someone outside biomechanics can act on.

Okafor adds a constraint of her own. The club's pitching coaches have spent five years setting targets in laboratory units — a layback range here, a trunk-tilt range there — and they will read any markerless number against those ranges whether or not they are told not to. Ferreira realizes that his briefing has two audiences: the executives who must decide, and the coaches who will live with whatever numbers appear on their screens. He decides that whatever he recommends must say plainly which numbers can be compared with which, and must show one worked example of what goes wrong if they are not.

Ferreira's draft list of what the study does not establish runs to five items: agreement in games; agreement for professional adults; agreement for the vendor's current model and camera layout; agreement for hitting; and any link between either system's values and performance or injury. He suspects the list is too long to be useful and too important to shorten. He also suspects the most consequential issue is not in the study at all — it is whether the club will ever compare one system's numbers with the other's.

exhibits.note: Synthetic data. Assumptions: the pitcher's true value is constant; the markerless system reads 8° lower than the laboratory system for this variable; each system's typical error is about 2°. The −9° 'change' is almost entirely system offset.

assumptions: The club can afford either the external laboratory or the markerless installation for the coming year, but not both indefinitely.
The vendor's software version differs from whatever version, if any, was used in the published study.
Coaches currently use laboratory values to set individual targets.
questions: Summarize the study's design and main findings in three sentences that a non-specialist executive could not misread.
What does a CMC of 0.88–0.97 establish, and what additional statistic would you need before comparing an individual pitcher's values across systems?
Which features of the sample and setting limit generalization to professional pitchers measured in games? Which later studies address part of that gap, and how well?
What does the study not establish about hitting, about current vendor software, and about performance or injury?
Should the club run both systems for a year? State what that year would need to measure to change your answer.

perspectives.title: Continuity first
perspectives.text: Keep the laboratory this winter and add the markerless system in parallel on the same throws for a subset of pitchers. The published study shows the systems differ in discrete values; the club's own simultaneous data are the only way to estimate bias and limits of agreement for its athletes, software version and variables. Switching without them sacrifices five years of longitudinal series for a correction that is valid only on average.

perspectives.title: Switch, but never mix
perspectives.text: Adopt the markerless system now and treat this season as a new baseline. The study's own recommendation — separate norms per system — is a licence to build a markerless series, not a reason to wait. The error is not changing systems; it is comparing across them. Freeze laboratory values as history, stop referencing them in targets, and estimate the markerless system's typical error in the club's setting before flagging change.

perspectives.title: Validate the purpose, not the system
perspectives.text: Neither the study nor the vendor answers the club's real question, which is whether in-game values can detect changes of the size coaches care about. Define two or three decisions, estimate the system's in-game typical error and MDC for those variables, and adopt it only for variables where the MDC is smaller than the change of interest. Keep hitting out of scope until agreement for swing kinematics is shown.

case.application: The same critique applies to any measurement claim in player development: ask which variables were validated, against what reference, in what athletes and setting, with what statistics, and for what decision. A study can be well designed, honestly reported and still not support the use a vendor or a colleague proposes. The discipline is to separate what the evidence establishes from what it is being used to justify.

questions.prompt: Laboratory A reports a pitcher's peak shoulder external rotation as 178°; Laboratory B, testing him a week later, reports 164°. Both have sub-millimetre calibration residuals. Which question should you ask first?

options.text: Which laboratory has more cameras?
Did the laboratories use the same humerus-relative-to-thorax rotation sequence and glenohumeral joint-centre method?
Was the pitcher's velocity higher in Laboratory A?
Which laboratory's residuals were smaller?

questions.explanation: Joint angles are computed through modelling choices: the rotation sequence and joint-centre estimate change reported shoulder rotation substantially. If those differ, the values are on different scales and the 14° gap may reflect definitions rather than the pitcher. Calibration residuals and camera counts concern reconstruction, the smallest error in the chain.

optionFeedback.a: Camera count affects occlusion and reconstruction, which are rarely the main source of cross-laboratory differences in joint angles.
optionFeedback.c: Velocity is worth knowing, but definitions must be shared before any change can be interpreted.
optionFeedback.d: Both residuals are already sub-millimetre; reconstruction is not the likely source of a 14° difference.

questions.prompt: Select every statement supported by the peer-reviewed markerless pitching studies covered this week.

options.text: Simultaneous capture of the same fastballs showed high waveform agreement between a markerless and a marker system.
The authors of that comparison recommended separate normative ranges for each system.
An in-stadium Hawk-Eye system was shown to agree with marker-based capture within 1° for shoulder rotation.
Within-pitcher variability was similar between in-game markerless and laboratory marker-based data for most, but not all, variables studied.
Markerless systems have been shown to be more accurate than marker systems for humeral rotation.

questions.explanation: Fleisig et al. (2022) reported CMC 0.88–0.97 and recommended system-specific norms; Lerch et al. (2025) found similar variability for eight of ten variables. Aguinaldo et al. (2025) found shoulder rotational variables agreed least, with per-joint position errors of about 52–57 mm; no study established that markerless capture is more accurate than marker capture.

optionFeedback.c: Aguinaldo et al. found shoulder rotation agreed least; no 1° agreement was reported.
optionFeedback.e: Agreement studies compare two imperfect systems; they cannot show which is closer to bone motion.

questions.prompt: What is the most important limitation of the validation claim in this fictional abstract?

stimulus.text: Fictional abstract. “We validated a markerless product we call System Z against marker-based capture in 12 recreational adults walking on a treadmill, recorded simultaneously at 120 Hz. Knee and hip flexion waveforms showed excellent agreement (CMC 0.95–0.98), and peak values were strongly correlated with the reference (r = 0.91–0.96). We conclude that System Z is valid for biomechanical assessment of athletes, including throwing.” Two authors are employees of the company that sells System Z.

options.text: The sample is too large.
Waveform similarity and correlation do not show that peak values agree; no bias or limits of agreement are reported for the variables a user would act on.
Gait is a more demanding test than pitching.
Sampling at 120 Hz is faster than necessary.

questions.explanation: CMC and correlation describe similarity of shape and ranking. A system can match patterns and rank athletes well while reading peak values many degrees off. A user comparing individual values needs the bias and limits of agreement for the discrete variables, in the task of interest, and the conflict of interest should be noted.

optionFeedback.a: Twelve participants is small, not large.
optionFeedback.c: Walking is slower and more planar than pitching; agreement in gait is an upper bound for throwing.
optionFeedback.d: 120 Hz is slow for pitching events; it is a further limitation, not an advantage.

stimulus.text: Synthetic. A pitcher's arm-worn sensor reports average fastball “elbow torque” of 72 N·m this week versus 66 N·m last week. Mound force plates show lead-leg peak vertical force up from 1.9 to 2.1 body weights, and his average fastball velocity is up 1.2 mph. A staff member writes: “UCL load up 9% — reduce volume.”

options.text: The pitcher's ligament load rose 9%, so his volume should be cut.

Estimated net elbow moment rose by an amount that may be within the sensor's error, alongside higher velocity; describe it, check the error, and leave load decisions to the medical and performance staff.
The sensor is broken because its values are lower than laboratory torque.
The force-plate increase proves the arm torque increase is real.

questions.explanation: The wearable estimates a net joint moment from one segment's kinematics and a model; it does not measure ligament load, and its published comparison found values correlated with but substantially lower than laboratory torque. Higher velocity is associated with higher estimated torque. Without the sensor's within-pitcher typical error, a 6 N·m change cannot be called real, and loading decisions are clinical.

optionFeedback.a: Net joint moment is not ligament load, and the change has not been shown to exceed measurement error.
optionFeedback.c: A consistent negative bias versus laboratory torque is expected from the published comparison; it does not mean the sensor is broken.
optionFeedback.d: Force plates measure a different quantity; agreement in direction does not validate the size of the torque change.

questions.prompt: In a test–retest study of peak lead-knee flexion at ball release, the standard deviation of the session-to-session differences is 4.2°. What is the typical error?
questions.explanation: Each difference score carries the error of two measurements, so its variance is twice the single-measurement error variance. Dividing the SD of differences by √2 gives the typical error of a single measurement.

questions.prompt: A field system's game-to-game typical error for a pitcher's peak shoulder external rotation is 3.0°. What is the MDC95?
questions.explanation: The change score between two occasions has error √2 × TE; multiplying by 1.96 gives the change that a stable athlete would exceed only 5% of the time. A change smaller than about 8.3° cannot be distinguished from error with 95% confidence.

questions.prompt: In a Bland–Altman comparison of two systems, the mean difference (System F − System L) is 6.0° and the SD of the differences is 3.5°. What is the upper 95% limit of agreement?
questions.explanation: Limits of agreement are bias ± 1.96 SD of the paired differences. For an individual measurement, System F is expected to read between about 0.9° below and 12.9° above System L, which is far too wide to swap the systems for decisions about individual athletes.

questions.prompt: What is the central flaw in this argument?

stimulus.text: “After our sequencing program, the hitter's average Statcast bat speed rose 1.8 mph and his attack angle rose 3°. The tracking data therefore confirm that his pelvis now leads his trunk by more, which is exactly what the program targeted.”

options.text: Bat tracking cannot measure bat speed.
Bat speed and attack angle describe the bat's motion; they cannot show how the body sequenced segments, so they cannot confirm a change in the kinematic sequence.
The hitter's sample of swings is too large.
Attack angle should be measured at the start of the swing.

questions.explanation: Tracking-derived metrics are outputs about the implement. A higher bat speed is consistent with many changes — or none — in pelvis and trunk sequencing, and attack angle also depends on pitch location. Claims about body kinematics require body measurement, from a validated system.

optionFeedback.a: Bat speed is a defined, tracked property of the sweet spot at contact.
optionFeedback.c: More swings improve the estimate of the bat metrics; the problem is what those metrics can represent.
optionFeedback.d: Statcast defines attack angle at contact; the definition is not the flaw.

questions.prompt: Rank these forms of evidence for the claim “the field markerless system can replace the laboratory system for measuring an individual pitcher's peak shoulder external rotation,” strongest first.

options.text: Correlation (r = 0.95) between the systems' values in a different sample of pitchers, each measured once by each system on separate days
Bland–Altman bias and limits of agreement from simultaneous capture of the same pitches in the club's own pitchers
A vendor press release stating accuracy “within 3°”
High waveform CMC from simultaneous capture in a published study, without discrete-value agreement statistics

questions.explanation: Simultaneous capture with bias and limits of agreement in the target athletes directly answers the interchangeability question. Simultaneous CMC removes athlete differences but addresses shape rather than values. A correlation across separate days confounds system with day-to-day variation and cannot establish agreement. A press release reports no methods.

questions.prompt: Which is the best next move?

stimulus.text: Synthetic. January laboratory value: 176°. Field markerless value in February: 168°; in April, after a drill block: 166°. Agreement data: field − laboratory bias −8.0°, limits −13.5° to −2.5°. Field typical error 2.1° (MDC95 ≈ 5.8°). The pitching coordinator wants to tell the player that the drills reduced his layback by 10°.

options.text: Report a 10° reduction in layback caused by the drill block.
Report that laboratory-to-field comparisons are not interpretable for individuals, compare like with like, and schedule a same-system retest.
Average the laboratory and field values to cancel the bias.
Discard the field system because it reads lower.

questions.explanation: The baseline and follow-up come from different systems with a −8° bias and wide limits, so most of the apparent 10° change is offset. Within the field system, the change from the February field value is 2°, below its MDC95 of about 5.8°. The defensible action is to compare within one system and retest.

optionFeedback.a: This attributes a cross-system offset to the drill.
optionFeedback.c: Averaging across systems produces a number that belongs to neither and does not remove the bias from the comparison.
optionFeedback.d: A known, stable bias does not disqualify a system for within-system monitoring.

questions.prompt: Why is surface EMG amplitude during arm acceleration not a valid measure of how much force the muscle produced?

options.text: Because EMG measures only fine-wire signals.
Because amplitude depends on electrode placement, crosstalk and normalization, and the EMG–force relationship changes with muscle length and velocity in dynamic tasks.
Because EMG cannot be filtered.
Because muscles are electrically silent during ballistic movements.

questions.explanation: Surface EMG records electrical activity under the electrode, contaminated by crosstalk and affected by tissue and placement. Even when normalized, its relation to force holds reasonably only in controlled isometric conditions; in throwing, muscle length, shortening velocity and electromechanical delay break the mapping.

optionFeedback.a: Surface EMG is a distinct method from fine-wire EMG and is widely used.
optionFeedback.c: EMG is routinely band-pass filtered, rectified and smoothed.
optionFeedback.d: Muscles are highly active during ballistic tasks; the issue is interpreting amplitude as force.

questions.prompt: A hitting coordinator wants to use the stadium's in-game markerless system to detect whether a hitter's pelvis-rotation timing changed after a two-week program. In 120–180 words, state what you would need to know or measure before accepting a reported change, and what the current peer-reviewed evidence on markerless hitting does and does not provide.
questions.modelAnswer: I would need the system's within-hitter typical error for this timing variable in games, estimated from repeated at-bats with no intervention, and from it the MDC95; the change must exceed that. Timing resolution matters: at the system's frame rate, event detection is uncertain by up to half a frame, so changes of a few milliseconds may be undetectable. I would also confirm no software or camera change occurred between periods and compare against pitch type and location, which alter swing timing. The peer-reviewed evidence includes a large in-game observational study relating hip–shoulder separation to bat speed within and between Division I batters, which shows such data can be analyzed at scale, but I found no peer-reviewed study validating markerless swing kinematics against a laboratory reference. So I can track change within the system once its error is known, but not claim the absolute values are accurate.

levels: 1 — mentions error without a same-system, in-game estimate
2 — requires within-hitter typical error and MDC in the setting of use
1 — names one (frame rate, software change, pitch context)
2 — names frame-rate limits and at least one other confound
0 — claims none exists or that it is validated
2 — notes the in-game observational study and the absence of a peer-reviewed agreement study

reserve.prompt: A pitcher cannot perform a controlled shoulder range-of-motion movement before testing. Which joint-centre approach is more practical, and what is its main cost?

options.text: Functional; it requires no movement
Predictive (regression from landmarks); it inherits the population and imaging assumptions of its equations
Functional; it cannot locate ball joints
Predictive; it requires biplanar radiography

reserve.explanation: Predictive methods need only a static trial with landmarks, so they work when a calibration movement is not possible, but they apply population equations that may not fit the individual. Functional methods need sufficient range of motion and are sensitive to soft-tissue artifact during that movement.

optionFeedback.a: Functional methods require the very movement the pitcher cannot perform.
optionFeedback.c: Functional methods are designed for ball joints.
optionFeedback.d: Predictive methods use palpated landmarks, not radiography.

reserve.prompt: Assume a bat–ball contact lasting 1 ms. On average, how many video frames fall within contact at 480 frames per second?
reserve.working: Frame interval = 1/480 s = 2.083 ms; expected frames in 1 ms = 1 / 2.083 = 0.48.
reserve.explanation: Expected frames during an event equal its duration times the frame rate. At 480 Hz fewer than half of swings will have any frame during a 1 ms contact.

reserve.prompt: A gyroscope has an uncorrected bias of 0.2°/s. How much orientation error accumulates over 90 s of integration?
reserve.explanation: Integrating a constant rate bias produces orientation error that grows linearly with time, which is why sensor fusion uses gravity and magnetic references and why throwing sensors re-reference frequently.

reserve.prompt: A study reports ICC = 0.91 for a markerless variable in a sample of youth to professional pitchers. What does this mainly tell you?

options.text: The variable can detect a 2° change in one professional pitcher.
Measurement error is small relative to the between-pitcher spread in that heterogeneous sample, which inflates ICC.
The markerless system agrees with marker capture.
The ICC form does not matter at this value.

reserve.explanation: ICC is the ratio of between-subject variance to total variance; a sample spanning youth to professional athletes has large between-subject variance, so ICC is high even with moderate error. Detecting change in one athlete requires the typical error and MDC; agreement with another system requires a Bland–Altman analysis; and the form must always be reported.

optionFeedback.a: Individual change detection depends on the typical error, which ICC alone does not give.
optionFeedback.c: Reliability within one system says nothing about agreement with another.
optionFeedback.d: Model, type and definition change ICC values and must be reported.

assignment.title: Measurement System Fitness-for-Purpose Memo

brief.text: You lead applied biomechanics for a fictional professional club. The development department proposes buying System F, a fictional multi-camera markerless system sampling at 300 frames per second, for the club's spring complex and two affiliate stadiums. Its stated purpose is narrow: flag, for coach review, any in-season change in a player's mechanics that is large enough to matter. Coaches have told you the size of change they would act on for five variables. The vendor's materials say System F is “validated.” Your own staff ran a pilot: simultaneous capture against the club's laboratory marker system, and repeated in-game measurement of stable athletes. Write the memo that recommends whether, and for which variables, System F is fit for this purpose.

brief.caption: Pilot validation data for System F (synthetic)
headers: In-game typical error (mean of ≥ 10 pitches or swings)
rows: Pitching: trunk forward tilt at release
Hitting: stride-foot contact to peak pelvis velocity
brief.note: Synthetic data for a fictional system and club. Pilot: 14 pitchers and 12 hitters for agreement (laboratory, simultaneous capture); 20 athletes for in-game typical error. MDC95 = 1.96 × √2 × typical error.

brief.text: Use the week's statistics explicitly. Distinguish what the pilot shows about agreement (needed only if you will compare with laboratory values) from what it shows about in-game reliability (needed for within-system monitoring). Note the frame interval at 300 Hz when you judge the timing variable. State what the peer-reviewed literature does and does not add, especially for hitting, and do not treat the vendor's word “validated” as evidence.

assignment.deliverable: A 900–1,300-word memo recommending, variable by variable, whether System F is fit to flag in-season mechanical change, with conditions and a monitoring plan.

template.heading: Recommendation
template.guidance: Three to five sentences: adopt, adopt for some variables, or do not adopt; for which purpose; the main condition.

template.heading: The decision and its measurement requirement
template.guidance: Restate the purpose and translate it into a requirement: the system's in-game MDC must be smaller than the change coaches would act on, and comparisons must stay within one system.

template.heading: Variable-by-variable assessment
template.guidance: For each of the five variables, compare MDC95 with the change of interest, comment on bias and limits of agreement, and conclude fit / conditionally fit / not fit. Address frame-rate limits for the timing variable.

template.heading: What the evidence does and does not establish
template.guidance: Place the pilot alongside the published markerless literature (pitching agreement studies; the state of hitting evidence). Separate vendor claims from peer-reviewed findings.

template.heading: Risks and safeguards
template.guidance: Software updates, camera changes between stadiums, mixing systems, coaches' expectations from laboratory values, and any temptation to read loading or injury meaning into the outputs.

template.heading: Monitoring and re-evaluation plan
template.guidance: How you will version-stamp data, re-estimate typical error each season, and what result would change your recommendation.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Uses MDC versus change-of-interest for every variable, distinguishes bias and limits of agreement from typical error, and explains which matters for within-system monitoring.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Uses MDC and agreement statistics correctly for most variables with minor confusions.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Uses some statistics but conflates agreement with reliability or relies on ICC-like reasoning.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Does not use the pilot statistics or misinterprets them.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Reaches defensible, differentiated conclusions (e.g., fit for knee flexion, borderline for trunk tilt, not fit for shoulder ER or pelvis velocity) and handles the timing variable's frame interval.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Differentiated conclusions with one weakly justified call.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Treats the system as wholly fit or unfit without variable-level reasoning.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No variable-level judgement.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Accurately represents published markerless pitching agreement studies and the absence of peer-reviewed hitting agreement studies; treats vendor claims as claims.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Mostly accurate, with a minor overstatement.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Overstates or understates the literature in a way that affects the recommendation.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Relies on the vendor's description or misstates the research.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Specific safeguards for software versions, cross-system comparison and loading misinterpretation, with a re-evaluation trigger.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Sound safeguards with limited specificity.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Generic risks without safeguards.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Risks not addressed.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: A non-specialist can act on the recommendation from the first section; terms defined; no hedging beyond what the evidence requires.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Clear with minor jargon.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Recommendation buried or ambiguous.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No clear recommendation.

prompts: Name one biomechanical or tracking number you have relied on in a decision. What was its typical error in the setting where it was collected, and did you know it at the time?
Where in your own environment are values from two different systems, or two software versions, being compared as if they were on one scale?
Which instrument in this week's lessons would you trust most for a within-athlete decision about hitters, and which least? What would change your ranking?
How would you explain to a coach, in two sentences, why a 5° change in a pitcher's layback might not be a change at all?

review.front: What does a marker-based system measure directly, and what does it model?
review.back: It measures 3D positions of skin markers by triangulation; segment orientation, joint centres, joint angles and moments are modelled.

review.front: What is the dominant error in skin-marker estimates of bone motion?
review.back: Soft-tissue artifact: skin and muscle moving relative to bone. It is subject- and task-specific and worst for long-axis rotations.

review.front: Functional versus predictive joint centres: one advantage and one cost of each.
review.back: Functional: individualized, but needs adequate range of motion and is sensitive to soft-tissue artifact. Predictive: needs only a static trial, but applies population equations.

review.front: Why does a clean angle signal produce a noisy angular acceleration?
review.back: Each differentiation multiplies noise by roughly the sampling rate; at 240 Hz, 0.8° angle noise becomes hundreds of °/s in velocity and over 10⁵ °/s² in acceleration unless filtered.

review.front: What is a markerless keypoint, and why is it not a joint centre?
review.back: A network's estimate of a labelled visual point; training labels are human visual judgements of joint locations, not anatomical centres.

review.front: What did Fleisig et al. (2022) find and recommend?
review.back: On 275 fastballs from 30 pitchers captured simultaneously, waveforms agreed (CMC 0.88–0.97) but discrete values differed systematically; separate norms per system.

review.front: What exists, peer-reviewed, on in-game markerless hitting (as of Nov 2026)?
review.back: Large observational work (e.g., 3,958 swings by 247 Division I batters relating separation to bat speed); no peer-reviewed markerless–marker agreement study of swing kinematics was found.

review.front: How is centre of pressure computed, and when is it unreliable?
review.back: From the plate's moments divided by vertical force; unreliable when vertical force is small, so a force threshold is applied.

review.front: Why do IMU orientation and position drift?
review.back: They are integrals of angular velocity and acceleration; constant biases grow linearly (orientation) or quadratically (position) with time.

review.front: What does a wearable elbow-torque sensor output?
review.back: A modelled net elbow moment from one segment's kinematics plus assumed arm properties; correlated with but lower than laboratory torque in a published comparison; not ligament load.

review.front: Why is EMG amplitude not muscle force?
review.back: It reflects electrical activity under the electrode, affected by placement, crosstalk and normalization; in dynamic tasks length and velocity change force for the same activation.

review.front: Degrees per frame for a 7,000°/s rotation at 240 Hz?

review.back: The vertical direction in which the bat's sweet spot is travelling at contact (or projected contact on a miss).

review.front: A 1-frame synchronization offset at 240 Hz with the bat at 32 m/s displaces the bat by about how much?

review.back: TE = SD of test–retest differences / √2; MDC95 = 1.96 × √2 × TE ≈ 2.77 × TE.

review.front: Why can ICC be high while a measure cannot detect change in one athlete?
review.back: ICC is between-subject variance over total variance; a heterogeneous sample inflates it without reducing the typical error.

review.front: What do Bland–Altman limits of agreement tell you that correlation cannot?
review.back: The bias and the range within which 95% of individual differences between methods fall, in measurement units.

Week 3 applies them to the lower body and trunk in pitching: ground reaction forces from mound plates, pelvis–trunk sequencing from 3D capture and energy-flow analyses built on inverse dynamics — each of which inherits the joint-centre, filtering and synchronization issues you studied here. Week 7 returns to tracked bat metrics and collision physics, and Week 12 extends this week's reliability statistics into the design of intervention studies, where the question becomes not only whether a change is real but whether something caused it.
